Specially arranged and rung to congratulate Tom Freeston on being given a Civic Award for “Service to the Community” by Boston Borough Council. This was awarded for his long and loyal service as Bell Ringing Captain at St Botolph’s (Boston Stump) and for services to bell ringing across the district. This will be awarded at a special ceremony on 18th April.

Tom has been Bell Ringing Captain at Boston Stump for 41 years, standing down at the end of last year, and has been ringing at the Stump for 66 years. He has also been President of the Eastern Branch of the Lincoln Diocesan Guild standing down last week at the AGM. Congratulation’s Tom, you deserve it! Especially for climbing the 209 steps up the Stump each week!

On Friday 15th February Hathersage Tower rang a 1/4peal in thanks to Mr Frank Stone, a long- standing member of the team, but who, due to illness, has not been able to attend ringing at church and regrettably is unlikely to be able to ring again.

Frank is well known in the village, not just as a bell ringer, but more particularly country wide as a guest of Adolf  Hitler resident at Stalag Luft III.  For the past 30 years Frank has been sharing his experiences of the camp explaining all the planning leading up to the great escape.
We will miss Frank very much.  Not only for his ringing but for his reliability in attending and in particular ringing the Tenor.  Not bad for 91 year old!

Rung open in celebration of the life of Anthony (Tony) Clifford.

Tony was taught to ring at St Mark's Cheltenham on a tied bell as the wartime ban on ringing was still in force. He became a staunch member of the band when the ban was lifted and a competent Doubles ringer. He enjoyed ringing at Swindon Village which was then a 5 bell tower and rang in the Quarter Peal there to celebrate the marriage of Queen Elizabeth to Prince Philip in 1947.

He continued ringing for some time until his work involving unusual hours caused him to give up. Unfortunately he could not take it up again in later life as he suffered from ill health, but he always spoke fondly of the good times and friendship he had enjoyed as a ringer.

Rung to commemorate the 70th anniversary of the Dambusters Raid, 16th/17th May 1943, on the Ruhr Valley Dams by 617 Squadron which was based at and flew from RAF Scampton.
Rung with the bells half muffled in memory of the 133 airmen who participated in the raid, but especially remembering the 53 aircrew who were killed during the raid.

Rung also remembering especially “Barnes Wallis” who came up with the concept and developed the bouncing bombs used in the raid. “Wing Commander Guy Gibson”, Commanding Officer of 617 Squadron who led the raid and finally “Nigger”, Guy Gibson’s black labrador retriever who was the mascot of 617 Squadron. Nigger died on the morning of the Dambusters Raid, 16th May 1943, when he was hit by a car outside RAF Scampton. Nigger was buried at RAF Scampton at midnight at the request of Gibson whilst he was leading the raid.

This is truly a community event and the conductor took part in this as a pupil of the school some years ago!

The peal was rung in memory of Seamus Heaney (1939-2013) Nobel laureate (Prize for Literature 1955)for whom bells were rung at Oxford and in Grahamstown during his visits to the universities in both cities. During his visit to Rhodes University in 2002 Heaney processed with the robed Vice-Chancellor, staff and students, from the University to the cathedral where he read some of his poems in the candlelit building: every pew was full and many students stood in the aisles. After the reading there was another procession to the Parish Hall for tea, during which all ten bells were rung. Heaney expressed great pleasure when told that the bells had rung in his honour. 'I suppose the next time will be when I am laid to rest', he said. The ringer of the second organised the ringing at Grahamstown and promised Heaney that, if at all possible, bells would be rung: 'when you are laid to rest'. '
